name: Han dynasty (Western Han)

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 4,567,000 km2 for 100 BCE (mid); the Wikipedia Han infobox gives Taagepera's 6.0 million for the 50 BCE peak (high). The world_bc100 Han Empire polygon measures 2.64 million km2 on the sphere (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aourednik/historical-basemaps/master/geojson/world_bc100.geojson, low); it omits much of the Hexi/Western Regions reach.

population.note: Seshat codes 45-60 million for the early Western Han and 57,600,000 for 1 CE; the 2 CE census counted 57,671,400 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_dynasty, high). At 100 BCE, after three decades of Emperor Wu's wars and the famines of the 110s, the population was below the 2 CE level; mid 45M is an estimate.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Chang'an 250,000-400,000 (Seshat 251), Luoyang, Linzi, Handan, Chengdu; mostly rural.

activePersonnel.note: Chang 2007 pp. 86, 186: standing army 400,000 early in Wu's reign, later 600,000-700,000 including ~300,000 cavalry, over 400,000 of them professionals; at least 150,000 professionals by 97 BCE.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess: men who had completed the two-year service were liable to annual recall (Bielenstein 1980 p. 114 via the Military of the Han page) out of a 13-15M draft pool.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Ship crews, frontier supply columns (Zhao Chongguo needed 1,500 carts a month for 10,281 men, Di Cosmo via the Military of the Han page), staff.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. Chang 2007 p. 86 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_of_the_Han_dynasty): a draft pool of 13-15 million men, ~30% of the population, under Wu. Total-war mobilisation of the whole population is a fraction of that; low/high span 4-12%.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Chang 2007 p. 86: cavalry rose from 80,000-100,000 to 200,000-250,000 before 124 BCE and ~300,000 later. Horse archers are the larger part; the split with heavy cavalry is an educated guess.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: composite bows and crossbows, horses from 36 state pastures

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: professional cavalry of the Wei Qing/Huo Qubing era

count.note: Educated guess. Armoured lancers; the 13 BCE arsenal inventory lists 5,330 horse armours (Military of the Han dynasty page), so only part of the cavalry was barded.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: iron lamellar, long lances

count.note: Educated guess. Halberd and spear infantry trained five ranks deep (Peers via Military of the Han page).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: 587,299 iron lamellar suits and 451,222 long lances in the 13 BCE inventory

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: one year of training, one of service, then annual recall

count.note: Educated guess. Crossbowmen; several hundred thousand crossbows in service (Needham via Military of the Han page).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75-1.0. Evidence: crossbows of 76 kg draw and more, the best missile weapon of the era

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: conscript crossbowmen

count.note: Educated guess. Paroled convicts and frontier auxiliaries (over 130,000 convicts drafted 111-97 BCE, Chang 2007 p. 186).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5 minus. Evidence: light kit

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: convicts and levies

count.note: Educated guess. Louchuan tower ships of the river and coastal fleets; Lo Jung-pang cites 200,000 seamen for the 112 BCE deck-ship fleet (Military of the Han page), a mobilised peak.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: multi-deck tower ships, river-optimised

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: conscript crews

count.note: Educated guess. Small river and coastal craft used against Nanyue (112) and Gojoseon (109).

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: conscript crews

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.75 (proven commanders). Evidence: Wei Qing and Huo Qubing broke the Xiongnu 127-119 BCE; Li Guangli's Ferghana war 104-101 was costly

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.5-0.75. Evidence: conscript core plus professionals, convicts and nomad auxiliaries

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.5-0.75. Evidence: victorious but war-weary; heavy losses in the 119 BCE campaign (Han-Xiongnu wars page)

weapons.note: Anchor: 3 (300 BCE). Evidence: mass iron weapons, crossbows of 76-340 kg draw (Loades via Military of the Han page)

armor.note: Anchor: 3 (iron cuirass, mail). Evidence: iron lamellar mass-produced (587,299 suits listed in 13 BCE)

ships.note: Anchor: 3 (quinqueremes). Evidence: louchuan tower ships, sea-borne invasions of Nanyue and Gojoseon

fortification.note: Anchor: 3. Evidence: frontier walls and forts extended to Dunhuang and Juyan

logistics.note: Anchor: 3 (depot system). Evidence: tuntian military colonies, documented ration scales (Juyan slips)

communications.note: Anchor: 3 (mounted relay posts). Evidence: relay posts and beacon lines along the Hexi corridor

isr.note: Anchor: 3. Evidence: beacon towers, frontier watch posts, Zhang Qian's missions to the west

gdpPerCapita.note: Analogue: Maddison 2023 (via OWID grapher CSV, https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true) has no China value before 1000 (1,225); its year-1 values for other agrarian empires are Egypt 1,116, Iran 1,116, France 956 (2011 int$). Early imperial China placed in that band, below the Song level.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Chang 2007 p. 118 (Military of the Han page) costs a 600,000-700,000 man army at 1.1-3.4 times annual state revenue of 12-20 billion cash, i.e. the wars ran deficits; mid is a wartime share of GDP.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. State iron and salt monopolies from 117 BCE; mass arms production.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. North China plain and Sichuan agriculture; military farms on the frontier.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the classical snapshots.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Qin imperial highways plus Han extensions to the Hexi corridor and the south.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. Panyu, Langya, Jiaozhi, Bohai coast ports.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Coastal trade; no figures.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Steppe campaigns of 1,000+ km (119 BCE) needed 140,000 supply horses and lost most of them (Han-Xiongnu wars page).

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. State herds of ~300,000 horses rising to over 450,000 under Wu (Chang 2007 pp. 174-175, Military of the Han page) plus private oxen and horses.

homeDefense.note: 1.2 row: fortified cities, frontier walls and dense population support at home.

notes: Snapshot 100 BCE, late in Emperor Wu's reign, after the Ferghana war. Force sizes follow Chang 2007 (Fall of Imperial China), the only modern quantitative reconstruction found; it is generous. Population convention: everything inside the empire; the 57.7M of the 2 CE census is the high bound. Ships are platform counts; their crews are supportPersonnel. GDP per capita is a regional analogy (grade D). Personnel: active = professionals plus conscripts serving their year (Chang's standing army); trainedReserves = discharged men liable to annual recall; mobilizable = population x ratio.
